title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
text:
GitHub Actions has become the go-to tool for automating workflows—whether you’re running tests, building reports, or deploying applications. It’s powerful, integrated, and for public repositories, completely free.
But here’s the catch:
GitHub Actions free tier only works for public repositories.
If your repository is private, you’re limited to about 2,000 minutes per month on the Free plan. Public repositories? Unlimited minutes. The same applies to GitHub Pages—deploying a website from a public repo is free, but deploying from a private repo requires upgrading your account.
So what do you do when your code contains:

Proprietary algorithms?
Client data that can’t be exposed?
Research methods not ready for publication?
API keys or sensitive configurations?

Most people think they have two choices:

Make the repository public (and risk exposing everything)
Pay for private repo minutes

But there’s a third way—and it’s smarter than both.

title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
section: The Solution: Public Workflow, Private Code
text:
The Solution: Public Workflow, Private Code
Here’s the key insight: Your workflow configuration doesn’t need to live in the same repository as your code.
You can create a public repository that hosts only your GitHub Actions workflows, while your actual code stays locked in a private repository. The two communicate securely using Personal Access Tokens (PATs).

Why This Works
✅ Your proprietary code stays private
✅ You get unlimited free GitHub Actions minutes
✅ You can showcase your automation process
✅ Outputs (reports, dashboards) can be published without exposing source code
✅ Perfect for reproducible research where methods are confidential but results should be shared

title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
text:
Real-World Example: Automated Weekly Reports
Let me show you how this works with a concrete scenario.

The Challenge
A healthcare organization needed weekly automated reports. The workflow required:

Connecting to a secure database (private credentials)
Running R-based data transformations (proprietary algorithms)
Generating a Quarto report
Publishing the final HTML to a public website

The problem: All code had to remain private, yet automation was needed every Monday morning—without exceeding free GitHub limits.


The Solution
Private Repository: client-health-pipeline

Contains: R scripts, data transformations, credentials
Status: Fully private

Public Repository: automated-reporting

Contains: Only the .github/workflows/ folder
Status: Public (to access unlimited free minutes)
Purpose: Triggers automation, connects securely to private repo, publishes results



The Outcome
✅ Private code remains protected
✅ Reports generate and publish automatically
✅ Zero additional GitHub costs
✅ Workflow transparency maintained
This approach works for automated reports, R package testing, ETL jobs, Shiny app deployment, and reproducible research—combining security, automation, and cost efficiency.

title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
text:
Step-by-Step Implementation

Step 1: Create Your Private Repository
This is where your actual work lives.
# Create a new private repository on GitHub
# Name it: my-private-analysis
# Initialize with a .gitignore
What goes here:

All your source code
Data processing scripts
Configuration files
Any sensitive information

Critical: Add a .gitignore file:
# Credentials and secrets
.env
.Renviron
config.yml
*.key

# Data files
data/raw/*
*.csv
*.xlsx

# Outputs
output/*
cache/*


Step 2: Create Your Public Workflow Repository
This repository will be public and contain only automation logic.
# Create a new PUBLIC repository
# Name it: automated-workflows
What goes here:

.github/workflows/ folder with your YAML files
Optional: README explaining your automation approach
Optional: Sample scripts (no sensitive code)



Step 3: Generate a Personal Access Token (PAT)
Your public workflow needs permission to access your private repository.

Go to GitHub Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic)
Click “Generate new token (classic)”
Name it: workflow-private-repo-access
Set expiration: 90 days (for security)
Select scopes: ✅ repo (full control of private repositories)
Click “Generate token”
Copy the token immediately (you won’t see it again!)



Step 4: Add the Token as a Secret
In your public workflow repository:

Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions
Click “New repository secret”
Name: PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN
Value: Paste your PAT from Step 3
Click “Add secret”

Security note: Secrets are encrypted and automatically redacted from logs.


Step 5: Create Your Workflow
In your public repository, create .github/workflows/automated-report.yml:
name: Weekly Report Generation

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * 1'  # Every Monday at 6 AM UTC
  workflow_dispatch:      # Allows manual trigger

jobs:
  generate-report:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
      - name: Checkout private code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: yourusername/my-private-analysis
          token: ${{ secrets.PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN }}
          path: private-code
      
      - name: Setup R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: '4.3.0'
      
      - name: Install R packages
        run: |
          cd private-code
          Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("tidyverse", "purrr"))'
      
      - name: Run analysis
        run: |
          cd private-code
          Rscript analysis.R
      
      - name: Render Quarto report
        run: |
          cd private-code
          quarto render report.qmd
      
      - name: Upload report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: weekly-report
          path: private-code/output/report.html
      
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
        with:
          github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          publish_dir: private-code/output


Step 6: Test Your Workflow

Go to the Actions tab in your public repository
Select your workflow
Click “Run workflow” (manual trigger)
Monitor the execution logs
Security check: Ensure no secrets appear in logs

title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
text:
Other Powerful Use Cases

Automated Testing for Private R Packages
Run R CMD check on every commit without exposing source code:
name: R Package Check
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: yourname/private-r-package
          token: ${{ secrets.PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN }}
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
      - run: R CMD check .


Scheduled Data Pipeline Execution
Run ETL jobs daily without manual intervention:
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'  # 2 AM daily
jobs:
  etl:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run data pipeline
        run: python etl_pipeline.py


Reproducible Research Workflows
Generate manuscript outputs while keeping methods confidential:
- name: Render manuscript
  run: quarto render manuscript.qmd
- name: Publish results only
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: published-paper
    path: output/manuscript.pdf


Shiny App Deployment
Deploy Shiny apps from private code to public servers:
- name: Deploy to shinyapps.io
  env:
    SHINYAPPS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SHINYAPPS_TOKEN }}
  run: |
    Rscript -e 'rsconnect::deployApp()'

title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
text:
What You Can Publish Safely
Even with private code, you can share:
✅ Final reports (HTML, PDF)
✅ Data visualizations and dashboards
✅ Documentation about your methodology
✅ Workflow configurations (YAML files)
✅ Logs (with sensitive info redacted)
What stays private:
❌ Source code with proprietary algorithms
❌ Raw data or personal information
❌ API keys and credentials
❌ Unpublished research methods
❌ Client-specific business logic

title: How to Use GitHub Actions Without Exposing Your Code
text:
Common Issues & Solutions

“Authentication Failed” Error
Cause: PAT doesn’t have right permissions or expired.
Solution:

Check token expiration
Regenerate with repo scope
Update secret in repository settings



“Resource not accessible by integration”
Cause: GITHUB_TOKEN can’t access private repos.
Solution: Always use PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN for private repo access, not the default GITHUB_TOKEN.


Secrets Appearing in Logs
Cause: Accidental print of sensitive variables.
Solution:
- name: Debug (safe)
  run: |
    echo "Workflow running..."
    # NEVER: echo ${{ secrets.PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN }}

Wrapping Up
Automation shouldn’t require compromising security. With this public-workflow, private-code approach, you get:
✅ Unlimited free automation

✅ Professional portfolio of your automation skills
This setup saves developers from the chaos of managing complex automations or exposing private code: reports generate automatically, data stays secure, and only polished results are shared.
Whether you’re a data scientist, researcher, or developer with confidential code, this pattern lets you embrace automation without exposure.

title: Beat Procrastination and Write Research Papers Faster
text:
Want to beat procrastination and draft faster?
Here are some of the most effective tips I’ve gathered that truly work.



Stop editing as you write! Your first draft is about getting ideas down, not grammar or polish.

Editing too early wastes time and fuels procrastination.

Save grammar, clarity, and formatting for later rounds.

✅ Perfectionism = procrastination. A rough draft builds clarity and momentum.




Here’s a plan that simplifies writing and saves time:

Structure first: Outline using your target journal’s template.

Write key sections first (Methods, Results).

Intro/Abstract last: they’ll be sharper once your content is final.

Draft fast: Aim for 1 section/day. Quarto’s dynamic formatting/code tools remove friction.

Revise after drafting: Polishing a full draft is faster and more motivating than fixing fragments.






Perfectionism slows you down — draft first, polish later.

Writing a rough Version 0 clears mental blocks and creates momentum.

Quarto Manuscript helps you stay focused on ideas, not formatting.


💡 Want to try these methods? Start with your next project: create a Quarto outline, commit to Version 0, and watch how much faster your draft grows.

Thanks for stopping by! Hope you found something useful :)

title: A Quick and Safe Way to Share Quarto Reports with Restricted Users
text:
Sometimes you need to share your updated reports with a restricted group of people instead of publishing them openly. A practical and secure way is to automate sending your reports by email. With Quarto and R, you can render your reports, attach them as PDF or HTML, and deliver them directly to your recipients’ inboxes.
In this post, I will show you how to achieve this with R and Quarto, using Gmail as an example.



To allow R to send emails from your Gmail account, you must create a Gmail App Password. This is safer than using your main password.

Enable 2-Step Verification in your Google Account Security settings.

Go to the App Passwords page.
Choose the app and device (e.g., Mail → Other → “R script”).
Click Generate. Google will display a 16-character password.
Copy and save this password immediately, as it cannot be viewed again later.

This password is what you will use in your R script instead of your usual Gmail password.



Below is a complete R script that renders your Quarto report (report.qmd), produces PDF and HTML versions, and sends them as email attachments. You only need to replace the email addresses and the Gmail App Password.

# --- Load packages ---
library(quarto)
library(blastula)

# --- Step 1: Render your Quarto report into PDF and HTML ---
quarto_render("report.qmd", output_format = "pdf")
quarto_render("report.qmd", output_format = "html")

# --- Step 2: Create the email body ---
email <- compose_email(
  body = md("
  Hello,  

  The updated Quarto report is ready.  
  Please find both PDF and HTML versions attached.  

  Best regards,  
  Islem
  ")
)

# --- Step 3: Attach the reports ---
email <- add_attachment(email, file = "report.pdf")
email <- add_attachment(email, file = "report.html")

# --- Step 4: Send the email ---
smtp_send(
  email,
  from = "your_email@gmail.com",
  to = c("recipient1@example.com", "recipient2@example.com"),
  subject = paste0("Updated Report - ", Sys.Date()),
  credentials = creds(
    host = "smtp.gmail.com",
    port = 587,
    user = "your_email@gmail.com",
    use_ssl = TRUE
  )
)
# The app password will be requested interactively in a popup after running, no need to hard-code it




To make this fully automated:

On Windows, schedule the script with taskscheduleR.
On Linux/macOS, use cronR or add it to your system cron jobs.
Every time the script runs, your Quarto report will be rendered and sent to the selected users automatically.




Email automation is not the only way to share Quarto reports with restricted users:

Netlify with password protection: host your Quarto site and restrict access with a password.
GitHub Actions or GitLab CI: automate report rendering and emailing or publishing.
Posit Connect: enterprise solution that provides user access control, scheduling, and automatic email notifications out of the box.

Choose the approach that best fits your context and your audience’s needs.



For many small teams or individuals, automating email delivery is a quick, safe, and effective way to share Quarto reports with a limited group of users. By combining Quarto, R, and the blastula package, you can render, attach, and distribute updated reports with minimal effort.

title: Islem Meherzi
text:
AI automation & data engineer

title: From RStudio to Published Paper: Writing Manuscripts with Quarto
text:
TipWhat You’ll Learn



By the end of this post, you’ll know how to write an entire research paper inside RStudio - complete with live code, auto-generated figures, formatted references, and multiple output formats (Word, PDF, HTML)- all from a single source file.
Time to read: ~8 minutes




If you’re a researcher using R and RStudio, you probably spend hours there every day: cleaning data, running analyses, creating visualizations, and building statistical models.
But then comes the hard part: writing the actual paper.
Suddenly, you’re juggling

Exporting figures to PNG files
Copy-pasting results into Word
Managing citations in Zotero or Mendeley
Updating figures when your data changes (again!)
Dealing with formatting chaos before journal submission

What if you could skip all of that?
With Quarto, your entire manuscript lives in RStudio alongside your code. When you update your analysis, your paper updates too—automatically. No more switching between tools. No more broken workflows.



Think of Quarto as the next generation of R Markdown, but supercharged:
✅ Works with R, Python, Julia, and Observable
✅ Creates Word docs, PDFs, HTML pages, and even journal-ready formats
✅ Handles citations, cross-references, and figure numbering automatically
✅ Already built into modern versions of RStudio (no extra installation needed!)
It’s designed for exactly what you’re trying to do: turn your research into a publication-ready document.






Note



New to R Markdown? Don’t worry! Quarto is beginner-friendly. If you can write in Word and copy-paste code, you can write with Quarto.





Let’s create a manuscript project in RStudio. It takes about 30 seconds:



In RStudio, go to: File → New Project
Choose: New Directory → Quarto Manuscript
Name your project (e.g., my-paper)
Click Create Project

RStudio creates a complete manuscript structure for you:
my-paper/
├── index.qmd          # Your main manuscript file (text + code)
├── references.bib     # Bibliography file (citations go here)
├── _quarto.yml        # Project settings (formats, styles, etc.)
└── my-paper.Rproj     # RStudio project file



Open index.qmd and click Render. You’ll see a beautifully formatted manuscript with:

Title and author information
Sections (Introduction, Methods, Results, etc.)
Example code chunks
Auto-generated bibliography

That’s it! You now have a working manuscript template.






Tip💡 Prefer to Start with a Complete Example?





I’ve created a ready-to-use template with a demo research paper example (including plots, tables, and references).
Download: quarto-manuscript-demo on GitHub
Just download, open in RStudio, and click Render. Follow the README for required instructions.







The index.qmd file is where your paper lives. Here’s what a simple manuscript looks like:






NoteClick to view complete example manuscript code





---
title: "Impact of Exercise on Sleep Quality"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2025-10-03"
format:
  html: default
  docx: default
  pdf: default
bibliography: references.bib
---

## Abstract

We investigated the relationship between exercise frequency and sleep quality in 200 participants over 12 weeks.

## Introduction

Sleep disorders affect millions of people worldwide [@smith2020]. 
Recent evidence suggests physical activity may improve sleep outcomes...

## Methods

### Data Collection

We recruited participants aged 25-65 and tracked their exercise habits using wearable devices.


::: {.cell}

:::


## Results

As shown in Figure 1, we found a positive correlation between exercise and sleep quality (r = 0.45, p < 0.001).

## References






YAML Header (the --- section at top): Contains your paper’s metadata
Markdown Sections: Use ## for main sections, ### for subsections
Code Chunks: Wrapped in ```{r} ... ``` — runs when you render
Citations: Use [@smith2020] to cite references from your .bib file
Figure Labels: #| label: fig-name creates numbered, cross-referenceable figures







Important



Tip: Use echo: false in code chunks to hide the code and show only the output. Perfect for final manuscripts!






One of the biggest pain points in academic writing is citation management. Quarto makes it surprisingly simple.



Create a .bib file (already done if you used the template!)
Add references in BibTeX format
Cite them in your text using [@citationkey]
Render → Quarto generates a formatted bibliography automatically




In references.bib:
@article{smith2020,
  title={The Science of Sleep and Exercise},
  author={Smith, Jane and Johnson, Mark},
  journal={Journal of Health Research},
  year={2020},
  volume={15},
  pages={234-245}
}
In your manuscript:
Recent research shows strong correlations [@smith2020].
Result: “Recent research shows strong correlations (Smith & Johnson, 2020).”



Want APA? MLA? Nature? Just add one line to your YAML:
csl: apa.csl
Download any citation style from Zotero’s style repository(16,000+ styles available!).






Tip💡 My Personal Workflow: Building References with Zotero





Here’s how I build my .bib files in under 5 minutes:

Install Zotero desktop app  (free reference manager)
Install Zotero browser connector to save papers with one click
While browsing a paper online, click the Zotero extension → automatically saved!
Export your library as BibTeX:

Right-click your library → Export Library → Choose “BibTeX (.bib)”
Save as references.bib in your manuscript folder


Done! Quarto will read it automatically. No manual typing of citations needed.
Why Zotero? It’s free, cross-platform, syncs across devices, and integrates beautifully with Quarto, Word, and LaTeX.







The magic moment: turning your manuscript into a finished document.


Option 1: Click the Render button in RStudio (top of editor)
Option 2: Run in terminal: quarto render



After rendering, check your project folder. You’ll find:
_manuscript/
├── index.html          # Beautiful HTML version
├── index.docx          # Microsoft Word document
├── index.pdf           # Professional PDF
└── index_files/        # Supporting files (figures, etc.)
All three formats generated from the exact same source file.



Open index.html in a browser. In the top-right corner, you’ll see an “Other Formats” section:



The “Other Formats” menu lets readers download your paper as Word or PDF with one click.


This means:

🌐 HTML for sharing online (blogs, lab websites)
📄 Word for co-authors and supervisors who prefer track changes
📕 PDF for journal submissions





Let me tell you why researchers who switch to Quarto never go back:


No more: “Wait, which version of Figure 3 did I send to my co-author?”
Your code, analysis, figures, text, and references are all in one file.



Changed your data? Re-run the analysis. Render again. Every figure, table, and statistic updates instantly.




Send collaborators the Word file for comments
Keep the .qmd source as your master version
Incorporate feedback and re-render




Other researchers can download your project, run quarto render, and recreate your entire paper—figures, tables, statistics, everything.



Quarto is plain text. It’ll open in 20 years. Try opening a Word 2003 .doc file today. Good luck. ==> Quarto’s use of plain text makes it future-proof, unlike closed, proprietary formats that may become obsolete.



Quarto can output to:

JATS XML (for journal submissions)
LaTeX (for traditional publishers)
Jupyter notebooks (for teaching)





Here’s what a complete Quarto manuscript looks like in practice:

Title & Authors with affiliations and ORCID IDs
Abstract with keywords
Introduction with citations
Methods section with inline code showing your analysis
Results with auto-numbered figures and tables
Discussion interpreting findings
References automatically formatted in your chosen style
Supplementary Materials (appendices, extra figures)

All of this renders to professional HTML, Word, and PDF formats.
See it in action: Download my complete example manuscript to explore the full structure.



Ready to write your next paper in RStudio? Here’s your roadmap:

Install/update RStudio (Quarto comes built-in)
Create a new Quarto Manuscript project
Explore the template structure
Add your data and analysis code
Write your manuscript sections
Add references to references.bib
Cite them in your text with [@key]
Render to HTML, Word, and PDF
Share with collaborators!







Tip



Stuck or want to learn more?
Check out the official Quarto documentation, it’s excellent and beginner-friendly!





Most researchers already live in RStudio for their analysis. Why not stay there for writing too?
With Quarto Manuscript, you can:

Write your paper where your code lives
Update figures and results automatically
Manage citations effortlessly

Export to any format your journal requires
Make your research fully reproducible

The best part? Once you set it up, writing becomes easier. No more juggling tools. No more version control nightmares. Just research, writing, and results: all in one place.
Start small: take one section of your current paper and try writing it in Quarto. You’ll immediately see why this approach is the future of academic writing.

Thanks for reading! If you found this helpful, download the demo template and give it a try. Feel free to reach out if you have questions, happy to help!

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
text:
The question I set out to answer was simple: can n8n actually orchestrate an R workflow end to end — not just trigger a script, but coordinate R, an API layer, a reporting tool, and an AI step into one pipeline that runs on its own?
Data profiling became the test case, because it’s a workflow I run often, and one where the raw output is genuinely hard for a non-technical person to use as-is. The point of this post is what happens when you let a handful of tools, each good at one job, get orchestrated together instead of stitching everything together manually.
R already does the hard part well. Packages like skimr and DataExplorer, or a simple Plumber API, can generate detailed quality metrics in seconds. That was never the problem.
The real challenge comes afterward. A JSON file filled with hundreds of metrics tells you what happened, but not what matters. So the shape I landed on was: let R handle the analysis, n8n orchestrate the workflow, Plumber expose the API, Quarto generate the report, and AI add the final layer by turning raw metrics into a concise narrative people can actually read.
That same architecture can power data validation, ETL monitoring, quality checks, or almost any R workflow that ends with “here are the numbers.” Data profiling just happened to be the first place I put it to the test.






Note



The AI never sees the raw data. It only ever sees a structured summary: aggregate stats, detected issues, metadata, quality scores.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
text:
Why that boundary matters
Keeping the LLM limited to the structured summary, never the raw rows, pays off in a few concrete ways:

Faster. A small JSON file, not a dataset, so response time doesn’t depend on file size.
Cheaper. Cost tracks the summary, not the row count: a 2-million-row file costs about the same to interpret as a 2,000-row one.
Privacy-friendly. No data leaves the R/Docker boundary: useful anywhere data protection rules apply (in Tunisia, the INPDP reform makes this less optional than it used to be).
Deterministic where it counts. Every number in the report came from R. The AI can explain a number, never invent one.
Less room for hallucination. Summarizing a dozen known facts is a narrow task; “analyze this dataset” is not.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
section: The stack, and what n8n does with it
text:
The stack, and what n8n does with it
Each piece here does one job. n8n is what turns them into a single pipeline instead of five disconnected tools.
R does the actual work: profiling, validation, duplicate detection, type inference, cleaning. Every number in the final report comes from here, and nothing downstream is allowed to override that.
Plumber turns the R script into an HTTP API, so n8n can call it directly instead of shelling out to Rscript (which breaks easily on path and environment issues):
#* Profile an uploaded dataset
#* @param file:file Uploaded CSV
#* @post /profile
function(file) {
  df <- readr::read_csv(file$datapath)
  metrics <- run_profiling(df)   # your existing profiling logic
  jsonlite::write_json(metrics, "metrics.json", auto_unbox = TRUE)
  metrics
}
n8n calls /profile, gets JSON back, and never needs to know R is even involved. That decoupling is what let me swap profiling logic underneath it several times without touching the orchestration at all.
Docker runs the pipeline as two containers:n8n in one, and the R/Plumber/Quarto service in another that handles both profiling and report rendering. This isn’t a formality: it’s what stopped “works on my machine” scripts from breaking the moment I moved environments, and it’s what makes the whole thing portable to any VPS.
n8n is the orchestrator that actually ties the above together. It receives the upload and email through a webhook, calls the Plumber API, sends the resulting JSON to the LLM, triggers the Quarto render, and emails the finished report. None of these steps is clever on its own — what n8n buys you is not having to hand-write retry logic, error branches, and conditional flow for each one.
OpenRouter handles the AI call, routed through one API that can reach DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, or GPT-compatible models. Switching models is a one-field change in one n8n node, no prompt rewrite required.






Tip



For full data privacy, swap OpenRouter for a local Ollama model. Same architecture — only the endpoint changes.


ngrok, optionally, exposes a local n8n webhook to the internet during testing: useful before you’ve deployed to a server.
Quarto renders the profiling metrics and the AI narrative into one HTML or PDF report, the same tool this blog runs on, for the same reason: reproducible documents without a separate templating layer.

Here’s what that looks like running for real in n8n:



AI-Powered Automated Data Profiling & Quality Report Generation


Here’s what that graph actually does: the webhook writes the upload to disk, then calls the R container’s /profile endpoint. n8n reads metrics.json back off disk, reshapes it, and feeds it to a Basic LLM Chain node pointed at OpenRouter for the narrative. That narrative gets posted back to the same R container — this time hitting its /report endpoint. n8n reads the finished report off disk, emails it, and responds to the original webhook.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
section: What the AI layer is actually allowed to do
text:
What the AI layer is actually allowed to do
The AI does: summarize results in plain language, prioritize which issues matter most, explain the practical risk behind a metric, produce next-action recommendations, flag anomalies worth a human look.
The AI does not: compute any statistic, decide what counts as a violation (that’s an R rule), see a single raw row, or override a business decision.
Every recommendation traces back to a number R already computed. It’s a communication layer, not a computation layer.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
section: Why deterministic-plus-AI beats “just use AI for everything”
text:
Why deterministic-plus-AI beats “just use AI for everything”
Feeding a raw dataset straight to an LLM and asking for a quality report is tempting, and I tried it early on. It falls apart for a few predictable reasons: validation stops being auditable, results stop being consistent run to run, and business rules end up buried in a prompt instead of visible in code.
Keeping R deterministic and the LLM strictly an explanation layer avoids all three, and it matters most in regulated environments, where “why did the system flag this?” needs an answer better than a fluent-sounding AI summary with no logic behind it.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
text:
What about agentic AI?
Agentic workflows: an LLM that plans its own steps, calls tools, and decides what to do next, are getting a lot of attention, and for genuinely open-ended tasks, that autonomy earns its keep.
For a pipeline like this one, it doesn’t, for three reasons:

Speed. An agent chains several LLM calls per task. This pipeline makes one: read the summary, produce the interpretation.
Hallucination compounds. Each extra autonomous step is another chance to misread something, and that error carries forward. One narrow call has far less room to go wrong than a multi-step agent deciding its own process.
The task is already solved. R already knows exactly how to compute profiling, validation, and duplicate checks, the same way, every time. An agent rediscovering that from scratch adds cost without adding value.

Agentic approaches make sense on the other kind of problem: look at this new dataset and tell me what’s odd about it,” where no rule set exists yet. That’s not this. For known metrics and defined rules, a deterministic core with an AI layer for summarizing and flagging has been the better trade-off.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
text:
Triggers beyond a manual upload
Once the webhook exists, the trigger is arbitrary: a new file landing in a folder, a scheduled nightly run, a change in SharePoint, Google Drive, or OneDrive, an S3 event, a database update, a Git commit. Each one produces a fresh report with zero change to the profiling or interpretation logic.

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
section: What it actually costs to run
text:
What it actually costs to run
This was deliberate from the start, not an afterthought. R, Docker, Plumber, Quarto, and n8n (self-hosted) are all open source, no licensing cost anywhere. The LLM call runs entirely on free-tier OpenRouter models, in practice: metrics.json is a small, well-defined input, and free models handle that kind of structured reasoning well.
Paid APIs are an option if you want more polished phrasing at scale, but they’re not required to get useful output. Swap in local Ollama instead of OpenRouter and it’s still zero, at the cost of your own compute. What used to require statistical training to interpret now runs on its own, for free — and it scales just as well from a solo analyst to a nightly production job.
Here’s what actually lands: the email as received, and a snippet of the report itself. For this run, I used a public dataset — the Messy Employee Dataset on Kaggle — so the metrics and issues you’ll see below are reproducible if you want to try the pipeline yourself.






The email delivered automatically, report attached







A section of the generated report, R metrics next to the AI narrative

title: Orchestrating R With n8n, Then Adding an AI Layer on Top
text:
Where this leaves things
This covers the architecture at the level that matters for understanding why it works: n8n orchestrates R, Plumber, and Quarto into one pipeline; R stays deterministic; the AI layer only ever sees a structured summary; and every component is open source or free to run. It’s the shape of the system, not a step-by-step build guide.
There’s enough underneath this: self-hosting n8n with Docker, webhook and node setup, structuring the OpenRouter prompt around the metrics schema, triggering the Quarto render, wiring up email delivery, that each one probably deserves its own writeup. I’m planning to follow up with a more hands-on post covering the setup in more detail, likely starting with the parts that are trickiest to get right.

Thanks for reading this far. If this setup is close to something you need, or you want a similar automated workflow built for your own use case, I’m happy to talk it through. You can reach me here.
